lessonTitle: Thermal and Fluid Models: Capacitance, Resistance and Linearisation

blocks.text: A cast-aluminium heating block on a laboratory hotplate takes nearly half an hour to warm up, while a thin-film sensor on the same hotplate reaches temperature in seconds. A coolant header tank drains slowly when its outlet valve is nearly shut and quickly when it is open. Both behaviours are first-order: a store (thermal mass or tank area) charging or draining through a resistance (convection or a valve), and the time constant is simply their product.

blocks.markdown: Thermal and fluid systems are modelled with the same lumped idea used for electrical circuits. A **capacitance** stores a conserved quantity (heat energy or liquid volume), and a **resistance** relates the flow of that quantity to a driving difference (temperature or head). The conservation law for the stored quantity gives the differential equation: rate of change of storage equals inflow minus outflow.

blocks.caption: Capacitance, resistance and time constant in three domains

blocks.markdown: **Thermal body with convective loss.** Consider a body of mass $m$ (kg) and specific heat $c_p$ (J/(kg K)) at a uniform temperature $T$ (K) (the lumped assumption, valid when internal conduction is much faster than surface convection). It receives heater power $q_{in}$ (W) and loses heat by convection to surroundings at $T_\infty$ with heat-transfer coefficient $h$ (W/(m$^2$ K)) over area $A$ (m$^2$). The energy balance is below. Writing $\theta=T-T_\infty$ gives $C_{th}\dot\theta+\theta/R_{th}=q_{in}$, a first-order system with DC gain $R_{th}=1/(hA)$ (K/W) and time constant $\tau=C_{th}R_{th}$.

blocks.caption: Energy balance and transfer function from heater power to temperature rise above ambient.

blocks.title: A heated block
blocks.prompt: An aluminium block of mass $m=0.5$ kg (typical $c_p=900$ J/(kg K)) loses heat with $h=15$ W/(m$^2$ K) over $A=0.04$ m$^2$. It is heated by $q_{in}=30$ W from ambient. Find the time constant, the steady-state temperature rise, and the rise after 600 s.

steps.text: Capacitance: $C_{th}=mc_p=0.5\times900=450$ J/K. Conductance: $hA=15\times0.04=0.6$ W/K, so $R_{th}=1/0.6=1.667$ K/W.

blocks.answer: $\tau=750$ s, $\theta_{ss}=50$ K and $\theta(600\ \text{s})=27.5$ K; the block needs about 29 minutes to reach 90% of its final rise.

blocks.markdown: **Liquid level in a tank.** A tank of constant cross-section $A$ (m$^2$) has inflow $q_{in}$ (m$^3$/s) and outflow $q_{out}$ through a resistive outlet. Conservation of volume gives $A\,dh/dt=q_{in}-q_{out}$. For a laminar (linear) resistance, $q_{out}=h/R$, with $R$ in s/m$^2$, so the tank is a first-order system with time constant $\tau=AR$ and DC gain $R$. A turbulent orifice or valve gives the nonlinear relation $q_{out}=k\sqrt{h}$ instead.

**Linearisation.** Most real component equations are nonlinear, but the transfer-function tools require linear ones. If $y=f(x)$ and the system operates near a steady point $(x_0,y_0)$, the first-order Taylor expansion gives $y\approx y_0+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)$. In terms of deviations $\delta x=x-x_0$ and $\delta y=y-y_0$ the model is $\delta y=f'(x_0)\,\delta x$, with a slope that depends on the operating point. The linearised model is accurate only for small excursions about $x_0$.

blocks.caption: Linearisation and the equivalent resistance of an orifice outlet.

blocks.title: Linearising an orifice-drained tank
blocks.prompt: A tank of area $A=0.5$ m$^2$ drains through $q_{out}=k\sqrt h$ with $k=0.002$ m$^{5/2}$/s. It operates at $h_0=1.0$ m. Find the linearised resistance, the time constant and the transfer function. Then check the prediction for a 10% rise in inflow.

steps.text: Operating flow: $q_0=0.002\sqrt{1.0}=0.002$ m$^3$/s, which is also the steady inflow.
Time constant $\tau=AR=0.5\times1000=500$ s, and the linearised model is $A\,\delta\dot h=\delta q_{in}-\delta h/R$, with $H/Q=1000/(500s+1)$ (m per m$^3$/s).

Check: a 10% rise in inflow is $\delta q_{in}=0.0002$ m$^3$/s, so $\delta h_{ss}=R\,\delta q_{in}=0.2$ m. The exact nonlinear steady state is $h=(0.0022/0.002)^2=1.21$ m, a rise of 0.21 m, so the linear model is within 5%.

blocks.answer: $R=1000$ s/m$^2$, $\tau=500$ s, $H/Q_{in}=1000/(500s+1)$; the linearised prediction (0.20 m) is within 5% of the exact nonlinear rise (0.21 m) for a 10% inflow change.

items: Choose the stored quantity (energy or volume) and write the conservation law for the lumped body.
Write the flow relationships (convection, outlet valve) in terms of the driving difference.
If a relationship is nonlinear, linearise it about the operating point using $f'(x_0)$.
Use deviation variables to obtain a first-order model $\tau\dot y+y=Ku$ with $\tau=RC$.
Check the assumptions (uniform temperature, constant area, small deviations).

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Mixing absolute and deviation variables: the transfer function relates deviations from the operating point, not absolute values. The resistance of a turbulent valve changes with the operating level, so $R$ (and $\tau$) from one operating point cannot be reused at another. For thermal systems, use $T_\infty$ as the reference or write the model in $\theta=T-T_\infty$; do not drop the ambient term. The lumped model fails if the Biot number $hL/k_s$ is not small.

blocks.title: Same structure everywhere
blocks.text: A capacitance filled through a resistance is a first-order lag with $\tau=RC$ in every domain, so the step-response results (63.2% at $\tau$, 90% at $2.3\tau$) transfer directly from electrical circuits to heating blocks and tanks.

points: Thermal body with convective loss: $mc_p\dot T=q_{in}-hA(T-T_\infty)$, a first-order system with $\tau=mc_p/(hA)$ and DC gain $1/(hA)$ K/W.
Tank with resistive outflow: $A\dot h=q_{in}-q_{out}$, with $q_{out}=h/R$ giving $\tau=AR$ and $h_{ss}=Rq_{in}$.
Linearising $y=f(x)$ about $(x_0,y_0)$ gives $\delta y=f'(x_0)\delta x$; for $q=k\sqrt h$ the resistance is $R=2\sqrt{h_0}/k=2h_0/q_0$.
Linearised models hold for small deviations around the operating point only.

questions.stem: A steel component of mass 2 kg (take $c_p=500$ J/(kg K), a typical value) cools in air with a convective conductance $hA=4$ W/K. Find the thermal time constant of the lumped model in seconds.
questions.explanation: The thermal capacitance is $C_{th}=mc_p=2\times500=1000$ J/K, and the time constant is $\tau=C_{th}/(hA)=1000/4=250$ s. The lumped model assumes a uniform temperature inside the component.

questions.stem: A body of heat capacity $C=mc_p$ is heated at $q$ watts and loses heat by convection with conductance $hA$ to ambient at $T_\infty$. Which differential equation gives its temperature $T$?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: stored energy rate equals heater input minus convective loss, which is proportional to the excess over ambient.
distractorRationale.b: The convective term has the wrong sign: it removes heat when $T>T_\infty$.
distractorRationale.c: The capacitance and conductance have been interchanged, so the units are inconsistent.
distractorRationale.d: The loss is proportional to $T-T_\infty$, not $T$; this version drops the ambient temperature.

questions.explanation: The energy balance is $C\dot T=q_{in}-q_{loss}$ with $q_{loss}=hA(T-T_\infty)$. In steady state $T-T_\infty=q/(hA)$, which has units of K when $hA$ is in W/K.

questions.stem: A tank is fed at a steady $q_{in}=0.004$ m$^3$/s and drains through a laminar outlet with resistance $R=250$ s/m$^2$ (so $q_{out}=h/R$). Find the steady-state liquid level in metres.
questions.explanation: At steady state $q_{out}=q_{in}$, so $h/R=0.004$ and $h=Rq_{in}=250\times0.004=1.0$ m. The tank area affects only how long it takes to get there, through $\tau=AR$.

questions.stem: A prismatic tank of cross-section $A$ has inflow $q_{in}$ and outflow $q_{out}=h/R$. Which differential equation describes the level $h$?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the volume balance $A\dot h=q_{in}-q_{out}$ with $q_{out}=h/R$.
distractorRationale.b: The outflow must be subtracted, since it removes liquid.
distractorRationale.c: The area multiplies $\dot h$ (volume change rate), not the right-hand side.
distractorRationale.d: The terms are mismatched: $R$ and $A$ are interchanged, so the units do not match.

questions.explanation: Conservation of volume gives $A\dot h=q_{in}-q_{out}$. Substituting the linear outlet law gives $A\dot h+h/R=q_{in}$, so the time constant is $AR$ and the DC gain is $R$.

questions.stem: A tank outlet obeys $q_{out}=0.003\sqrt h$ (SI units, $h$ in m and $q$ in m$^3$/s). Linearise about the operating level $h_0=0.64$ m and give the slope $dq_{out}/dh$ at that point in litres per second per metre (L/s per m; 1 m$^3$ = 1000 L).
questions.explanation: The derivative is $dq/dh=0.003/(2\sqrt h)$. At $h_0=0.64$ m, $\sqrt{0.64}=0.8$, so the slope is $0.003/1.6=0.001875$ m$^2$/s, which is 1.875 L/s per m. The linearised resistance is $R=1/0.001875=533$ s/m$^2$.

questions.stem: A drag force on a moving carriage is $F=0.8\,v^2$ (N, with $v$ in m/s). It operates near $v_0=5$ m/s. What is the linearised damping coefficient $dF/dv$ at this operating point?

distractorRationale.b: This forgets the factor 2 from differentiating $v^2$ (it gives $0.8\times5$).
distractorRationale.c: This is the operating force $F_0=0.8\times25=20$ N, not the slope.
distractorRationale.d: This is the coefficient in the nonlinear law, not the slope at $v_0$.

questions.explanation: Linearisation uses the derivative at the operating point: $\delta F=(dF/dv)|_{v_0}\delta v=2cv_0\,\delta v$. The effective damping therefore grows with speed, and the model is valid only for small speed deviations about 5 m/s.

questions.stem: A linearised model obtained about an operating point $(x_0,y_0)$ is reliable for small deviations from that point but may be inaccurate for large excursions.
questions.explanation: The first-order Taylor expansion neglects second- and higher-order terms, which grow with the size of the deviation. For example, an orifice-drained tank linearised at 1.0 m predicts the response to a 10% inflow change within 5%, but would give larger errors for a doubling of the flow.

questions.stem: The cross-sectional area of a tank with a laminar outlet resistance $R$ is doubled (same $R$ and same inflow). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The time constant doubles and the steady-state level is unchanged
The time constant is unchanged and the steady-state level doubles
Both the time constant and steady-state level double
The steady-state level halves and the time constant halves

questions.correctOptionText: The time constant doubles and the steady-state level is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\tau=AR$ doubles; $h_{ss}=Rq_{in}$ does not depend on $A$.
distractorRationale.b: $h_{ss}=Rq_{in}$ does not depend on $A$, so it does not double.
distractorRationale.c: Only the time constant is proportional to $A$.
distractorRationale.d: The level and time constant do not halve when $A$ doubles.

questions.explanation: The storage capacity (area) affects how long it takes to reach a steady level, $\tau=AR$, but at steady state the inflow equals the outflow $h/R$, so the level $Rq_{in}$ is independent of $A$.

questions.stem: Derive a first-order model for a lumped body heated by a power $q_{in}$ and cooled by convection to ambient, state the assumptions, and obtain the time constant and DC gain. Explain how the same structure appears for a tank with a resistive outlet.
markingGuide: Assumptions: uniform body temperature (small Biot number), constant $h$, $c_p$ and $T_\infty$
Deviation form $\tau\dot\theta+\theta=q_{in}/(hA)$ with $\tau=mc_p/(hA)$ and DC gain $1/(hA)$ K/W
Identifies capacitance and resistance correspondence ($mc_p\leftrightarrow A$, $1/(hA)\leftrightarrow R$)
questions.explanation: A complete answer emphasises the conservation law followed by a constitutive (flow-resistance) law. Recognising the common $\tau=RC$ structure lets thermal and fluid results be read from the first-order response.

questions.stem: Explain how to linearise the nonlinear outflow $q_{out}=k\sqrt h$ of a tank about an operating level $h_0$, give the resulting equivalent resistance, and discuss how the time constant of the linearised tank depends on the operating point and when the linear model should not be trusted.
markingGuide: Takes the Taylor expansion $\delta q=(dq/dh)|_{h_0}\delta h$ with slope $k/(2\sqrt{h_0})$
Linearised equation $A\delta\dot h=\delta q_{in}-\delta h/R$ with $\tau=AR$
$R$ and $\tau$ increase with $\sqrt{h_0}$ so the tank is slower at higher levels
Linear model is valid only for small deviations; large changes in level or inflow change $R$ and give errors
questions.explanation: The linearised time constant is not a property of the tank alone but of the tank and the chosen operating level. For large excursions the nonlinear equation should be simulated directly.
